entries.title: Remarkable releases new Capture Tool
entries.summary: The reMarkable software update 3.28 is a major system release that introduces highly anticipated tools, color improvements, and reading enhancements to digital paper tablets The post Remarkable releases new Capture Tool first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Remarkable software version 3.28 introduces a new Capture Tool and improved color rendering. The Capture Tool allows you to circle and select any area of a document, then duplicate, resize, rotate, or move that content across different pages or notebooks. Improves color rendering for red tones on color-supported devices for ballpoint, fine-liner, and calligraphy brushes, eliminating the need for a screen-refresh flash.

The new software also moves the sharing menu to the main toolbar for quicker access, without opening the three-dot menu. The update also includes serious enhancements to the reading experience. Remarkable has updated the EPUB reading experience with a UI uplift, improved formatting, and expanded language support. The updated interface makes it easier to choose fonts and layouts, while the new font options help improve readability. Formatting tweaks ensure a better layout and presentation throughout your ebooks. Ebook thumbnails also look nicer.

You can take a look at the entire change log here.

entries.title: New TCL P80 phones have NXTPAPER AMOLED display
entries.summary: The TCL P80 Ultra and TCL P80 Pro are hybrid smartphones designed to blend premium display performance with dedicated, e-reader-style eye comfort. The post New TCL P80 phones have NXTPAPER AMOLED display first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The TCL P80 Pro and TCL P80 Ultra are newly released smartphones that seamlessly combine traditional smartphone functionality with the eye-comfort benefits of an e-reader. Both feature TCL’s revolutionary NXTPAPER AMOLED display, which offers a matte, anti-glare finish, circular polarization, and significantly reduced blue light emission.

Both phones have a physical side slider that instantly transforms the interface into “Max Ink Mode”. This black-and-white, low-distraction mode cuts off heavy notifications and allows the battery to last up to 7 days for reading books. Both include intelligent reading assistants that can convert standard text e-books into podcast-style audiobooks.

The TCL P80 Ultra and TCL P80 Pro share identical foundational hardware centered around a 6.83-inch 1.5K (2772 x 1280) eye-friendly NXTPAPER AMOLED display. This matte, low-glare screen supports a fluid 120Hz refresh rate, 3,200 nits of peak brightness, and a physical chassis toggle to activate a low-power, monochromatic “Max Ink Mode”. Under the hood, both devices pack a massive 5,800mAh battery that supports 45W fast charging, 8GB of RAM, up to 512GB of internal storage, and an IP68 and MIL-STD-810H durability rating. They launch with Android 16 and a comprehensive software commitment of four major OS upgrades alongside seven years of security patches

The main hardware difference between the two models is their processing power and camera arrays. The flagship TCL P80 Ultra runs on the more capable MediaTek Dimensity 7400 Elite processor. It stands out with a versatile triple rear-camera setup: a 50MP main sensor with OIS, an 8MP ultra-wide lens, and a dedicated 50MP periscope telephoto lens with 3x optical zoom. Conversely, the mid-tier TCL P80 Pro scales back performance and imaging to hit a more affordable price point. It uses the lower-tier MediaTek Dimensity 7300 processor and omits the telephoto lens, dropping to a simpler dual-camera setup that keeps the same 50MP main and 8MP ultra-wide shooters.

The official launch prices for the TCL P80 series vary slightly by region and storage capacity. The TCL P80 Pro will cost approximately $500 to $580, and the TCL P80 Ultra will be $640 to $650. Both models are slated to hit regional markets and global storefronts like Amazon throughout September 2026.

entries.title: E Ink Carta 1400 might be pushed back to 2027
entries.summary: Industry sources have told Good e-Reader that the E INK Carta 1400 will be delayed until 2027, meaning Kaleido 4 and Gallery 4 won't be released anytime soon. The post E Ink Carta 1400 might be pushed back to 2027 first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
E-Ink’s Carta 1400 was previously rumored to debut later this year, but supply-chain sources have told Good e-Reader that the tech won’t be ready for mass production until later in 2027. E-Ink’s largest partners, including Foxconn, which makes the Amazon Kindle; Netronix, which manufactures Kobo and NOOK e-readers; and Linfiny, which focuses on B2B, have received samples of the new screen technology to see how it will fit into future e-readers.

E-Ink still has no Carta 1300 white papers or product listings on its own website, and the tech has been part of mainstream Kindle and Kobo e-readers for years. No information explains what Carta 1400 will bring to the table. Rumors suggest it will push the standard optical contrast ratio past 20:1 for crisp text. Lower latency will make page turning, scrolling, and handwriting feel much closer to an iPad or paper note. Higher contrast ratios deliver crisp, “truer” blacks and ultra-bright whites to maximize outdoor and low-light readability. Refined waveform technology to drastically minimize text ghosting and the dramatic “black flash” associated with full e-ink screen refreshes.

E INK Carta 1300 was known as an incremental, generation-on-generation refinement of Carta 1200. While Carta 1200 was a massive, ground-up architectural overhaul that introduced significantly faster refresh speeds to the e-paper industry, Carta 1300 builds on that same foundation to deliver slightly better contrast metrics and lower latency.

The delay of Carta 1400 will cascade to Kaleido 4 and Gallery 4, which are in the prototyping stage. This color E-INK technology will not come out until Carta 1400 is used in e-readers such as the Amazon Kindle Paperwhite and other black-and-white e-paper e-readers of the future.

entries.title: Acer Announces New ePaper Monitor
entries.summary: The Acer EP130K ePaper monitor is a portable, touch-enabled 13.3-inch display introduced at IFA 2026. The post Acer Announces New ePaper Monitor first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Dasung, Bigme, and several other brands have been involved in the e-paper monitor business for a long time. Recent entrants such as Philips failed to gain traction because demand was low. Acer hopes to leverage its household name with the Acer EP130K ePaper monitor that offers a paper-like visual experience ideal for reading and deep work, plus touch support, up to 3200 x 2400 resolution, and both color and black-and-white modes. It uses a Kaleido 3 e-paper display from E INK.

Combining the natural viewing experience of paper-like visuals with glare-free use, the new Acer EP130K is designed for professionals who perform deep work for long periods, avid readers, and mobile users whose work takes them outdoors. The monitor supports touch directly on its ePaper screen, enabling stylus use and the intuitive feel of writing or drawing with a finger. It delivers up to 3200 x 2400 resolution with a 60 Hz refresh rate, and offers both color and black-and-white modes to switch between as needed. A single USB Type-C cable supplies power from the host device to the low-power-consumption panel, while its bistable functionality keeps the on-screen image in place even when all power sources are removed.

The Acer EP130K ePaper monitor starts at $749.99 USD in North America, €749 in EMEA, and $1,499 AUD. It will launch in these markets in early 2027.

entries.title: Smart Glasses vs. Earbuds: Which Is Safer for Audiobooks on a Walk?
entries.summary: What are the best way to listen to audiobooks while on the go? Headphones, earbuds, or speakers on smart glasses? The post Smart Glasses vs. Earbuds: Which Is Safer for Audiobooks on a Walk? first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Most audiobook listeners follow a routine they never question: putting in earbuds, playing the book, and setting off on a walk. This habit has proven effective and has long been the norm, so the idea of changing the format rarely crosses most people’s minds. Yet, the global audiobook market reached US$8.3 billion in 2024, and a significant portion of listening occurs while walking or commuting, situations where listeners must simultaneously navigate the real-world environment. It is in this context that the choice of device shifts from a mere matter of audio quality to something far more significant. Smart glasses featuring open-ear audio are gaining popularity as an ideal solution for these scenarios; the reasons behind this are specific enough to warrant an accurate assessment, rather than a vague answer like “it depends on the situation.”

Smart Glasses Solve the Problem Earbuds Create

The safety issue regarding headphones while walking is more serious than most listeners have carefully considered. US data shows that serious pedestrian injuries involving headphone users tripled over a decade, with 70% of these incidents proving fatal, and a consistent finding is that victims failed to hear approaching vehicles or warning signals until it was too late. Noise-canceling headphones can reduce ambient noise by up to 45 decibels, enough to render a car horn inaudible at close range. A 2025 study in Transportation Research Part F confirmed that listening to audio while walking was the most common form of distraction among pedestrians aged 18 to 30. For audiobook listeners, the risk is compounded: not only are you unable to hear your surroundings, but you are also cognitively immersed in a narrative, effectively placing two layers of inattention between yourself and the environment. Smart glasses address this issue at its core rather than at the margins. Open-ear speakers built into the frame’s temples project audio toward the ear without blocking it, meaning that traffic, cyclists, warning signals, and conversations remain audible at their natural volume while the audiobook plays. Meta glasses use this open-ear approach to deliver clear spoken audio while helping listeners remain aware of nearby traffic and other warning sounds.

You aren’t choosing between the audiobook and your surroundings; you get both.

The Audiobook Experience Through Smart Glasses Is Better Than Expected

The first question most audiobook listeners ask about smart Meta glasses is whether the audio quality is actually good enough, and the honest answer is yes, it is more impressive than most people expect before trying them. The open-ear format has genuine limitations for music, where bass response and isolation matter. For audiobooks, which consist of well-produced human voices within a consistent frequency range, these limitations are largely inconsequential. The narrator comes through clearly at comfortable volumes, and after a few minutes, the open-ear format no longer feels different from what you are accustomed to. Among current options in this space, smart glasses integrated into performance frames have evolved to the point where audio delivery is truly practical for extended listening sessions, rather than just casual use. The frames sit on the face just like regular sunglasses; they are so lightweight that you stop noticing them within the first few minutes, and the controls for pausing, resuming, and adjusting volume, via voice commands or frame buttons, are reliable enough that managing playback doesn’t require stopping or reaching into your pocket. According to National Highway Traffic Safety Administration data on pedestrian safety, distracted walking involving audio devices accounts for an increasing share of pedestrian fatalities each year. Smart glasses alter the nature of this distraction by eliminating the auditory isolation that makes it dangerous, rather than simply asking listeners to be more cautious while wearing devices that actively hinder their ability to hear.

Practical Advantages Beyond Safety

While safety is the primary argument in favor of smart glasses over headphones when walking, it is not the only one. Their form factor offers practical advantages for audiobook listeners that headphones do not. You are already wearing the glasses when you leave the house, eliminating the need for a charging case, cable management, or the hassle of deciding whether they are worth the extra trouble. If someone speaks to you while you are walking, you can hear and respond to them without removing anything or needing to explain yourself. The constant process of taking headphones on and off for every social interaction during a walk is a minor annoyance that becomes significant when repeated daily over months. Smart glasses also better deliver on the promise of keeping your phone in your pocket: since navigation, calls, and basic AI queries are handled through the glasses, the phone actually stays in your pocket for most of the walk, rather than being constantly pulled out to manage audio playback. Furthermore, the open-ear design makes it easier to follow your safety instincts while walking; if you hear something unusual nearby, you immediately pick up the signal and can react. This ability to react is precisely what headphones are designed to block; for an audiobook listener walking in the city or on shared paths, this sacrifice is not worth it.

Where Smart Glasses Have Limitations Worth Knowing

An honest assessment of smart glasses for walking while listening to audiobooks must include their limitations, as these are real and worth knowing before making the switch. Battery life on current models supports several hours of audio playback on a single charge, comfortably covering most walking sessions, but it isn’t an all-day solution for listeners who also want to use the same device at a desk or on public transport. Charging the frames requires a conscious effort; unlike earbuds with a case that charges them automatically in your pocket, smart glasses require deliberate charging. The open-ear audio experience is also more dependent on the environment than that of standard headphones: a quiet park path offers a significantly better listening environment than a walk along a main road during rush hour. In noisier settings, you will need to increase the volume to compensate, which further reduces battery life. These are significant considerations, not minor details. For listeners whose daily walks take place in consistently noisy urban environments, headphones remain the superior option for pure audio quality, and the safety argument is the primary reason to consider making the switch anyway.

Who Should Use Smart Glasses and Who Should Wear Headphones?

According to annual sales data from the Audio Publishers Association, 74% of audiobook listeners consume content while engaged in another activity, with walking and exercising ranking among the top three contexts. This means that most audiobook listening occurs in environments where the choice of device has safety implications, not just audio preference considerations. Smart glasses are the right choice for listeners walking along roads, intersections, shared cycling paths, or in any setting where failing to hear an approaching object could lead to harm. The open-ear format handles audiobooks well enough that audio quality is not a significant reason to stick with headphones in those conditions. Headphones remain a valid choice for listeners whose walks take place in truly quiet, traffic-free environments, where the ambient sounds preserved by open-ear audio are not critical for safety, and the superior audio quality of in-ear listening is more important. The honest conclusion of this comparison is not that one device is universally better. Smart glasses are particularly well-suited for walking, the context in which most audiobook listening takes place, and this is a more useful conclusion than a general comparison of preferences.

Conclusion

Headphones became the go-to device for listening to audiobooks while walking because they were the best option available when the habit was formed. Smart glasses represent a truly different approach that addresses the specific safety issues headphones create for pedestrians, while simultaneously offering an audiobook experience good enough to make the switch worthwhile. For anyone who listens to audiobooks during walks involving traffic, shared paths, or urban environments, the case for smart glasses-based audio is strong enough to warrant serious consideration rather than just a passing thought. The audio sounds good. You can hear your surroundings. These two things turn out to be compatible, and the fact that headphones made them seem mutually exclusive for so long is more a product of habit than necessity.

entries.title: iReader Tango 2S is coming out soon
entries.summary: Like previous models in the Tango series, it is primarily targeted at Asian markets upon launch, with Western buyers usually relying on import options. The post iReader Tango 2S is coming out soon first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The iReader Tango 2S is an upcoming pocket-sized, smartphone-shaped e-reader with a 5.8-inch Carta 1300 screen at 300 PPI. iReader has shared a first look and teaser poster for the Tango 2S, but it has not yet finalized release dates or pricing. It follows the original iReader Tango (6.13-inch) and the Tango 2, making the Tango 2S the most compact model in the lineup.

iReader Tango is a specialized line of smartphone-sized, pocketable e-readers developed by the digital reading brand iReader (PalmRead). Designed to compete directly with devices like the Onyx Boox Palma, the Tango series is built for highly portable, single-handed reading.

The original model established the phone-like form factor. It features a 6.13-inch E Ink Carta 1300 display with a sharp 300 PPI resolution. It stands out with an octa-core processor, a massive 3,900mAh battery lasting up to 27 days on standby, and physical side page-turn buttons. It also introduced a 30Hz fast refresh mode to make scrolling smoother than traditional e-ink screens.

The Tango 2 is a direct, iterative successor, maintaining the 6.13-inch compact blueprint with minor hardware refinements. The newest addition shifts to an even more compact form factor, scaling down to a 5.84-inch display. It is marketed as the first 5.84-inch Carta 1300 monochrome screen to maintain a crisp 300 PPI pixel density.

entries.title: HyRead Gaze Pro Max C 13.3 e-note is available for pre-order
entries.summary: The HyRead Gaze Pro Max C is a 13.3-inch color e-paper device offering a large-format reading and note-taking experience, optimized for PDFs, magazines, and comics. The post HyRead Gaze Pro Max C 13.3 e-note is available for pre-order first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The HyRead Gaze Pro Max C is a large-format 13.3-inch color e-paper reader and e-note designed for reading PDFs, academic papers, magazines, and sheet music. It is available for pre-order in Taiwan until September 20th and costs about $793 during the introductory pre-order period; it will retail for about $914 when it becomes available to order.

The HyRead Gaze Pro Max C features a large 13.3-inch flat Kaleido 3 color e-paper screen. It uses T2000 fast-refresh technology to make page turns and scrolling smoother. A built-in front light lets you adjust between warm and cold color temperatures for comfortable reading in any room. The black-and-white resolution is 3200×2400 at 300 PPI, while the color screen is 1600×1200 at 150 PPI.

Under the hood, this device runs on Android 14, letting you install various legal apps and digital reading software. It runs an Octa-core (quad-core A72 + quad-core A53) processor and packs 8GB of RAM and 128GB of internal storage to hold your large PDF files, documents, and books. For wireless connectivity, it supports fast Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.2 alongside a versatile USB-C port.

Built-in dual speakers and four microphones for messaging, it is powered by a 5240mAh polymer lithium battery and supports PD fast charging.

If you want to read your own books, the device supports EPUB, PDF, MOBI, DOC, DOCX, TXT, FB2, RTF, HTML/HTM, DJVU/DJV, and CBR. Supported image compression formats: ZIP, RAR, and CBZ.

entries.title: Remarkable B2B Strategy is not paying off
entries.summary: Remarkable's B2B head has left the company, which casts serious doubt on its entire business strategy. The paper tablet simply doesn't meet enterprise customers' needs. The post Remarkable B2B Strategy is not paying off first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Paul Kagoo, General Manager of Enterprises & B2B at Remarkable, has left the company, casting serious doubt on the overall B2B strategy. Overall, the paper tablets are primarily aimed at consumers, and enterprise customers cannot use these devices at scale. Yes, it’s encrypted, but what if a vulnerability pops up in the Remarkable tomorrow that allows someone to bypass that encryption? Security teams have no way to mitigate or patch it, because they can’t.

Breaking into the enterprise market can be a significant challenge for niche devices. Companies have stringent governance protocols for adopting new technologies. Implementing a new device necessitates thorough risk management assessments and comprehensive data privacy reviews. Additionally, the IT department must onboard the device to ensure support, patching, and maintenance. Cybersecurity teams also need to build robust incident response and protection processes. All this effort often supports a relatively small group of users within the organization. And if we factor in regulatory requirements, the complexity grows even further.

The stark truth is that Remarkable devices currently in use in enterprise settings likely violate many corporate policies, yet people continue using them regardless. This puts ReMarkable in a difficult position for B2B sales. The costs of adopting new technology extend beyond the initial purchase; they also include a wide array of hidden expenses.

The big problem with ReMarkable is that it bills its tablets as distraction-free, which hampers their B2B ambitions. You can’t have any sort of viable B2B integration without supporting the Microsoft 365 suite. You need integration with Outlook too, but the company does offer support for Microsoft OneDrive and SharePoint integration alongside Google Drive and Dropbox. People may desperately want to deny it, but Microsoft is still the king of B2B operations systems and business workflows. Then secondly, you need to focus on the Google ecosystem, which they did first with Google Drive integration. But usage is clunky at best for an enterprise use case.

Ultimately, enterprise, B2B, and consumer users have drastically different requirements for the paper tablet. Businesses and security teams need access to the source code to make changes and AI tools to assist with meetings and notes; however, Remarkable doesn’t offer that. Most people agree that Remarkable should go back to basics and just target customers, which is their bread and butter, and forget about business.

Remarkable reached out to Good e-Reader and said the following “business sales have been an active part of how reMarkable operates for years and remain so. Businesses buy from us directly through the webshop, which handles what a procurement process needs out of the box — company details and VAT number captured at checkout, invoice issued automatically with the order confirmation, bank transfer alongside card and Klarna, and quantity discounts applied automatically from five devices. Our vendor registration details are published for procurement teams. Our business solutions team speaks with B2B customers daily and handles larger orders, tax-exempt quotes, evaluation units and enterprise terms. Published customers include Salesforce, UNESCO and Mainstreet Credit Union, to name a few. “

entries.title: Amazon has a new Fire Tablet that will come out soon
entries.summary: Amazon will likely release a 2nd generation Fire 11 Max Tablet sometime in the next few months, and it will be a substantial upgrade. The post Amazon has a new Fire Tablet that will come out soon first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
Amazon has just attained FCC certification to sell an upcoming Fire Tablet in the United States. This is typically the last step before a product can be released. Based on the posted specs, it is likely a 2nd-generation Fire 11 MAX, which hasn’t been available for purchase for several months.

A few key specs have been posted. It will be powered by a MediaTek MT8189, which is an 8-core ARM system-on-chip built to power upcoming budget and mid-range Chromebooks and tablets. It will have 8 GB of RAM and 64GB of internal storage, which isn’t enough by 2026 standards, but it will have an SD card to expand storage further. For comparison, the current Fire Max 11 has 4 GB of RAM, so 8 GB would be a pretty substantial upgrade.

entries.title: Brooklyn Public Library Launches Limited Edition Jay-Z Library Card
entries.summary: To mark the 30th anniversary of his groundbreaking debut album, Reasonable Doubt, BPL released the special "JAŸ-Z 30" limited-edition library card. The post Brooklyn Public Library Launches Limited Edition Jay-Z Library Card first appeared on Good e-Reader.
entries.content:
The Brooklyn Public Library has partnered with hometown icon Jay-Z and his entertainment agency, Roc Nation, on two major cultural collaborations. To mark the 30th anniversary of his groundbreaking debut album, Reasonable Doubt, BPL released the special “JAŸ-Z 30” limited-edition library card. Alongside the rollout, the Marcy Library branch in Bed-Stuy launched “JAŸ-Z’s Booklist”—a dedicated shelf featuring a curated list of books that heavily influenced the artist’s life and career.

The JAŸ-Z 30 Limited Edition Library Card follows the 2023 release of The Book of HOV library card collection, created in conjunction with The Book of HOV exhibition presented by Brooklyn Public Library and Roc Nation. The series featured 13 limited-edition cards highlighting artwork from JAŸ-Z’s studio albums, from Reasonable Doubt through 4:44.

The Book of HOV exhibition drew more than 600,000 visitors during its nearly five-month run at Brooklyn Public Library’s Central Library, making it one of the most attended public exhibitions in the institution’s history. The exhibition’s final day welcomed nearly 11,000 visitors—the highest single-day attendance recorded at the library—and contributed to a 74 percent increase in attendance at Central Library during its run.

The exhibition also introduced thousands of new users to library services. More than 36,000 The Book of HOV library card accounts were created, contributing to a 66 percent increase in new accounts systemwide and a more than 300 percent increase at Central Library. Among the original card designs, The Black Album was the most requested, followed by The Blueprint.
